title: Bazaine and Castelnau → Napoleon III, Mexico, French cipher cable of 373 cable words intercepted by Sheridan's telegrapher Charles A. Keefer, never deciphered
correspondents: Marshal François-Achille Bazaine and General Castelnau → Napoleon III (copy sent by Charles A. Keefer → Gen. U. S. Grant)
place: Mexico City (transmitted via the French consulate, New Orleans)
shelfmark: Keefer to Grant, New Orleans, 17 Dec 1866, William H. Seward Papers (University of Rochester), microfilm reel 98; copy also in the LC Grant material (Weber, Masked Dispatches ch. 17 n. 60)
folio_note: 373 cable words of French cipher copied by Keefer from the line; plain text of the same message printed by Georges Girard, La vie et les souvenirs du général Castelnau (Paris 1930), pp. 117-118
status: Weber (Masked Dispatches, 3rd ed. 2013, pp. 114-116 and n. 63): Keefer 'could not decipher it' and hoped for the plain text from a French newspaper; 'There is no evidence Keefer ever solved the French cipher.' The plain text was published in 1930, so the content is known; the French cipher system itself was never reconstructed. Not in the repo (known.py: Keefer, Bazaine no hits).
why: A rare surviving ciphertext of the French army/imperial cable cipher at the end of the Mexican intervention, with a published plaintext: a known-plaintext key recovery that would identify the system and read Keefer's other intercepts.
score_note: Scored from Weber, Masked Dispatches (NSA 2013) during the Oct 2026 NARA/State Department sweep (research/nara_state/); not viewed
verify: Locate Keefer's 17 Dec 1866 letter (Seward Papers reel 98; check whether Papers of Ulysses S. Grant vol. 16 prints the cipher); get Girard 1930 pp. 117-118 for the plaintext; align.
prior_art: partly: plaintext printed by Girard 1930; no decipherment of the cipher found (checked 27 Oct 2026: Masked Dispatches notes, web search)

title: US minister at Vienna → Secretary of State, cable in the 1867 State Department code with the code letters run together, 'never deciphered'
correspondents: US minister at Vienna (Henry M. Watts 1868-69 or John Jay II 1869-75; unknown) → Secretary of State (Seward or Fish)
shelfmark: NARA RG 59, Telegrams received by the Department of State (1867 code period; Entry 209 'State Department Telegrams 1867-1869' cited by Weber) or Despatches from US Ministers to Austria (M46); exact item not identified
status: John Haswell to Hamilton Fish, 8 Jul 1873 (Fish Papers reel 95, LC), quoted by Weber, Masked Dispatches pp. 106, 131: cables from Turkey (decoded by J. C. B. Davis after long labour), Paris and Vienna arrived as strings of connected code letters; 'the latter one was never deciphered'. The 1867 code (letters and groups of unequal length, telegraphers merged them) is known (Weber 1979 prints it).
why: A State Department cable that was never read in its own time; with the 1867 code known it is a segmentation problem, and it would show what the Vienna legation reported in the late Seward/early Fish years.
score_note: Scored from Weber, Masked Dispatches (NSA) during the Oct 2026 NARA/State Department sweep (research/nara_state/); not viewed
verify: Find the telegram: Despatches from Austria (M46, reels for 1867-73) and RG 59 telegram files; check Haswell's letter in the Fish Papers for a date; get the 1867 code from Weber 1979.
prior_art: open (checked 27 Oct 2026: Masked Dispatches; no item located)

title: German Foreign Office → Bernstorff (Washington), German cipher telegram forwarded through the US Embassy Berlin (Grew), text not printed in FRUS
correspondents: German Foreign Office → Count Bernstorff, German ambassador at Washington (via Chargé Joseph C. Grew → Secretary of State)
shelfmark: NARA RG 59, 1910-29 decimal file (World War I series; FRUS 1916 Supplement doc. 424)
folio_note: FRUS prints only Grew's covering telegram: '[German cipher. Not printed.]'
status: FRUS 1916 Supplement, The World War, doc. 424: Grew forwards 'the following cipher telegram which is said to relate to' the Washington talks; the German code text is omitted. German diplomatic traffic sent over the US channel in 1916-17 was in codes 13040/0075 and was largely read by Room 40, so a decrypt may exist in TNA (HW 7, ADM 223); not checked.
why: German code text passed by the State Department during the 1916 peace-note period; checkable against the Room 40 codebooks reconstructed for 13040.
score_note: Scored from the FRUS text during the Oct 2026 NARA/State Department sweep (research/nara_state/); not viewed
verify: Find the decimal-file copy (RG 59 763.72119 or 862.20212 series) on NARA; check Room 40 decrypts in TNA HW 7 / ADM 223 for 5 Dec 1916 before treating as open.

title: Robert R. Livingston → John Jay, Philadelphia, instruction passage in a modified Thomson code that the Jay Papers editors call 'undecipherable'
correspondents: Robert R. Livingston (Secretary for Foreign Affairs) → John Jay
shelfmark: ALS, partly in code, NHi Jay Papers (EJ 598); triplicate NHi; dup./quadruplicate NNC (EJ 7763, 7925); Dft NHi R. R. Livingston (EJ 1537); LbkCs NARA PCC item 79 vol. 1 pp. 332-34 and item 118 pp. 48-50 (M247)
folio_note: one passage (Livingston's attempt to add six symbols for syllables ending in r to the Thomson code); the rest of the letter was decoded by the editors from the draft
status: Selected Papers of John Jay vol. 2 (Founders Jay/01-02-02-0272) n. 7: 'RRL's passage is undecipherable, as explained in JJUP, 1: 664'; Jay could not decode either this letter or the 20 Oct 1781 one (code lost with William Palfrey). Founders sweep (research/founders_emlo) did not search 'undecipherable'.
why: Small, but it is the one passage of the Livingston-Jay correspondence that the modern edition could not read, in a nomenclator family that is otherwise reconstructed.
